question: Bound firms can buy cleaning, security and landscaping services from contractors with fewer than 50 FTE instead of employing full-timers.
rationale: Under K3, a firm's FTE count includes its own employees, plus firms under common control and agency workers, who count for the agency. A contractor's staff count toward the contractor. Nothing in the Act stops a bound firm from buying cleaning, security or landscaping as a service from an independent firm under 50 FTE, and such firms commonly exist in these trades. A-17 covers a narrower claim with p 0.55: firms near 50, at a cost below the term or the charge. This question asks only whether the purchase is possible, which is more likely. Some doubt remains about whether enough small contractors exist and whether some arrangements would be treated as common control.

question: Some bound employers can replace full-time jobs with more part-time jobs under 30 hours.
rationale: K1 applies only to employees averaging 30 or more hours a week, and part-timers under 30 hours are expressly exempt. Under K3 their hours still count toward the 50-FTE test, so splitting jobs does not take a firm out of the Act, but it does avoid the per-head term or charge. Many uncovered workers at bound firms are in retail, food service, cleaning and security, where shift work is easy to divide. The per-head cost is large: $1.44–$3.32 an hour. Splitting jobs brings its own costs (hiring, training, scheduling), and A-11 suggests full-time hours partly substitute for heads, which limits the response. Still, it is very likely that at least some bound employers can make this switch at a cost below the per-head cost. No assumption row states exactly this; the closest is A-10 (p 0.75), so I judge slightly above it.

question: Bound employers can cut other non-wage terms, such as training and schedule flexibility, where the wage cannot fall.
rationale: The record is silent on training, scheduling and other non-wage terms, and no assumption row states this claim. The Act only regulates the health offer (K1/K2), the minimum wage (R1) and overtime (R4). Other terms such as training, schedule flexibility, breaks and discounts are left to at-will contracts, so employers are legally free to change them. Where R1 binds (A-9) or wages are sticky in the short run (A-3), cutting other terms is the open margin for shifting the per-head cost. One limit is that low-wage jobs at minimum-wage payers may already offer few such terms to cut. The other is that cutting schedule flexibility can conflict with keeping workers under 30 hours. So the capacity plausibly exists for some bound employers, though not all.

question: Bound employers that offer cover prefer applicants who will decline it, such as those covered by a spouse's plan.
rationale: Under K1, a bound employer meets its obligation for an employee by offering cover, and 'An employee who is offered and declines counts as offered.' The employer pays its 70% share (about $5,180 a year) only for employees who enroll. An applicant who will decline, such as one covered by a spouse's plan, therefore costs the employer about $5,180 a year less than an equally productive applicant who will enroll, with no charge owed. Where wages cannot fall to absorb that difference, as at the minimum wage (A-9), the employer prefers the decliner. Above the minimum, wages could in principle differ, but pay scales make individual wage offsets hard (A-3). That leaves a preference in hiring among otherwise similar applicants. The record says nothing on anti-discrimination rules or on employers' ability to screen. The preference follows from the cost structure, though how far employers act on it is uncertain.

Still, 'some' bound employers being able to do it is more likely than not. This is close to A-17, which puts contracting out and franchising below the per-head cost at p=0.55, but that row covers a different arrangement. question: An employee averaging 130 or more hours a month counts as one FTE however many hours are worked.
rationale: K3 defines FTE as the number of employees averaging 130 hours a month, plus all other employees' hours divided by 130. Under that formula, each employee at or above 130 hours is counted once, whatever their hours, and only shorter-hours employees are converted by hours. No assumption-table row states this; the answer rests on the record text.

question: Some firms near 50 FTE can meet extra work by longer hours from existing full-timers, paying overtime, instead of hiring.
rationale: Under K3, any employee averaging 130 or more hours a month counts as one FTE no matter how many hours they work. Extra hours from existing full-timers therefore do not raise a firm's FTE count, while a new hire does. R4 makes hours above 40 cost 1.5 times the regular rate, so this route is dearer per hour but feasible. The claim needs only that some firms near the threshold can do this. That is plausible for many small service and production firms, which already use overtime routinely. A-11 covers substitution between 30 and 40 hours (p 0.65), not overtime above 40, so it is related but not the same statement. The record is silent on how much firms rely on overtime. From general knowledge, the existential claim is likely true, though limited by fatigue, the nature of the work and the overtime premium.

question: Crossing 50 FTE raises a firm's labour cost by up to $3,000 a year per uncovered full-timer.
rationale: Under K1 and K3, a firm at 50 or more FTE must either offer qualifying cover or pay $3,000 a year for each uncovered full-timer. Since paying is always open, the statutory cost per uncovered full-timer is at most $3,000. Offering costs at least $5,180 at the 70% share, so a firm would only offer if the worker values the cover. K4's cap and later wage pass-through can only push the net cost lower. The cost is a cliff: on crossing, it falls on every uncovered full-timer, not just the marginal hire. 'Up to $3,000' per head therefore matches the record. Remaining doubt concerns wording: compliance and reporting costs are extra, and the cost depends on the firm's average FTE over the prior year.

Under U1-a, about 380 firms with 30–49 year-round FTE would reach 50 only because seasonal hours count. For a part-month worker, FTE is hours ÷ 130, averaged monthly over the year. Some of these firms will sit just above the line, and trimming a modest number of seasonal hours in 2027 could bring them under. The main obstacles are output lost at peak season and overtime cost. Feasibility for at least some firms is still likely, consistent with A-14 (0.7).

question: Seasonal employers that offer cover prefer applicants who will decline it or who will leave before 60 days.
rationale: No assumption row states this directly; A-30 concerns shortening engagements, which is a different question. The answer follows from the cost structure of K1. For a bound employer that chooses to offer, each full-timer who accepts costs at least 70% of a $7,400 premium. An employee who is offered and declines counts as offered and costs nothing. An employee who leaves before 60 days is owed no offer. So, other things equal, such an employer gains by preferring applicants who decline or leave early, and the decline margin is the clearest case. Three caveats keep confidence moderate. First, preferring early leavers conflicts with staffing a season longer than 60 days and with retraining costs. Second, an employer can only partly screen for who will decline. Third, under U1-b some seasonal firms are not bound at all, though the question concerns firms that do offer.

question: Seasonal firms' profits are paid from their earnings on labour.
rationale: No assumption row matches this statement, and the record says nothing about where seasonal firms' profits come from, so this is judged from general theory. In a praxeological reading, profit is the gap between product prices and the prices paid for all factors. It rewards entrepreneurial appraisal of uncertain demand. It is not a deduction taken from labour's earnings. Wages tend toward the discounted marginal product of labour, so profit is not 'paid from' what labour earns. The record treats the 380 seasonal firms (farms, food processing, resorts, landscaping) only by their FTE count under U1 and their likely lack of cover (A-33). Nothing in it supports the exploitation-style claim.

K2 requires physician and prescription coverage with a deductible capped at $2,500, which lowers the out-of-pocket price of that care. The ICP pays hospitals, not outpatient physicians or prescriptions, so uninsured low-wage workers faced close to full price for this care. A rise in use is therefore likely. question: Owners of bound firms that pay the charge or add cover lose part of their firms' value and earnings.
rationale: For firms that pay the charge or add cover, K1 is a new per-head cost: $3,000 a year, or a 70% share of a $7,400 premium. Owners avoid losing earnings only if the whole cost passes to workers or customers, and the record argues against both. In the short run money wages are sticky (A-3, 0.75), so the cost falls on profits. The minimum wage blocks wage offsets for low-wage workers (A-9, 0.85), and the record says about 11% of private employees earn at or near it. Workers have some alternatives, so wages do not fall by the whole charge even in the medium run (A-8, 0.85). Passing the cost to customers is limited because unbound small, compliant and capped firms compete in the same local markets (A-22, 0.65), and most competitors are not bound at a material cost (A-24, 0.4). Since business values reflect expected earnings and buyers expected the Act from its introduction (A-21, 0.7), the earnings loss is capitalized into firm value. Capped firms pay up to $300,000 directly. Long-run shifting to wages may cut the loss, but the claim is only that owners lose part, which holds across most channels. The main doubt is whether the loss shows up in values as well as earnings.

rationale: The record says nothing about the market for buying businesses. Generally, though, buyers can put capital into many other assets at a market rate of return. So the price of a firm whose expected earnings fall under K1 (charge or cover cost) should fall roughly by the capitalized loss: buyers will not pay the old price for a lower earnings stream. This is a standard capitalization premise. It is close to A-21 (p 0.7) but not identical, because A-21 adds a claim about when buyers came to expect the Act. Some doubt remains because rent may fall on land, other sellers or workers rather than on the firm's value, and because thin markets for small firms can blunt the effect.

rationale: The record says nothing about physician or clinic supply or about insurer fee setting, so this rests on general knowledge at enactment. rationale: Cover at a bound firm adds compensation that a worker loses by moving to a firm under 50 FTE that offers none. In the short run, money wages are sticky (A-3), so cover at a 70% employer share is a net gain at the bound job, and leaving costs that gain. A-35 says some newly covered workers are near the stay-or-move margin, so the effect bites for some of them. Over the medium run, wages above the minimum can adjust (A-6). If wages fall by the full employer cost and workers value cover below that cost (A-7), the net pull of the bound job could shrink or even reverse. Minimum-wage workers' pay cannot fall (A-9), which keeps the retention effect for them. On balance the answer is yes, with uncertainty about medium-run wage offsets.

question: Each offer falsely reported in place of paying the charge reduces the K1 charges the Department of Revenue collects.
rationale: Under K1 a firm pays $250 a month for each full-timer it does not offer, and the charge is assessed from the offer status it reports on its quarterly withholding returns. A false offer report therefore removes that employee's charge from the assessment. Since the question specifies a false report made in place of paying, collections fall by that charge. There are two caveats. First, for capped firms well above 100 uncovered full-timers (K4), a false report would not change what they pay, but then no charge was being paid on the margin, so the question's framing excludes that case. Second, a detected false report triggers a penalty of twice the unpaid charge, which could more than offset the loss in those cases. Because verification is weak (A-18), most false reports are likely to go undetected, so the net effect per false report is a reduction in collections.
